S E C T I O N 1 O F 7
Foundations of Carbon Accounting
Before any formula: what exactly are we counting, and in what units?
05

S E C T I O N 1 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is a Carbon Footprint?
A precise, measurable quantity — not a metaphor.
Working Definition The total greenhouse gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by an organization, product, event, or 
individual, expressed in a single common unit.
Why "Carbon" When We Mean Several Gases CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide and others all trap heat differently — "carbon footprint" is shorthand for the 
combined warming effect of all of them together.
The Unit That Makes This Possible tCO₂e — tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. Every gas is converted into "how much CO₂ would cause the same 
warming," so they can be added together.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 06

S E C T I O N 1 · A C O M M O N C U R R E N C Y
Global Warming Potential (GWP): Converting Gases to CO₂e
1
Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) — the reference 
gas
27–30
Methane (CH₄) — over a 100-year 
period
273
Nitrous Oxide (N₂O) — over a 100-
year period
25,200
Sulfur Hexafluoride (SF₆) — over a 
100-year period
Formula: Mass of Gas (tonnes) × GWP = tCO₂e. This is what lets a factory's methane leak and a car's CO₂ exhaust sit on the same balance sheet.
Source: IPCC AR6 Working Group I (2021), 100-year Global Warming Potential values.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 07

S E C T I O N 1 · M O T I V A T I O N
Why Organizations Measure Their Footprint
Measurement is now a regulatory, financial, and strategic requirement — not a goodwill gesture.
Regulatory Compliance India's SEBI mandates BRSR (Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting) disclosure for the top 1,000 
listed companies by market cap, including Scope 1 and 2 emissions.
Carbon Markets India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), run by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, prices emissions directly —
you cannot trade what you cannot measure.
Investor & Customer Pressure Frameworks like CDP and the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) require verified Scope 1, 2, and increasingly 
Scope 3 data before certifying any climate target.
You Can't Manage What You Don't Measure Every reduction strategy — efficiency, renewables, supply-chain redesign — starts from a credible baseline 
number.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 08

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
A company emits 2 tonnes of methane (CH₄) in a year. Using a GWP of 
28, how many tCO₂e does this represent?
A 2 tCO₂e
B 28 tCO₂e
C 56 tCO₂e
D 280 tCO₂e
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. 56 tCO₂e
Mass of gas × GWP = tCO₂e. Here: 2 tonnes × 28 = 56 
tCO₂e. This is the exact calculation used to fold non￾CO₂ gases into a single footprint number.

S E C T I O N 2 O F 7
The GHG Protocol Framework
The global standard behind every "Scope 1/2/3" number you will ever see reported.
10

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E S T A N D A R D
The GHG Protocol: The Global Standard
Developed jointly by the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD).
What It Is The most widely used international accounting framework for measuring and reporting greenhouse gas 
emissions — the source of the "Scope 1/2/3" terminology used worldwide.
Who Uses It The overwhelming majority of Fortune 500 companies reporting emissions use the GHG Protocol as their 
accounting foundation, alongside frameworks like ISO 14064-1 which align closely with it.
Why It Matters For This Course Every calculation in this lecture — and every case study in this course — is built on this exact framework.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 11

S E C T I O N 2 · S T E P Z E R O
Setting Organizational Boundaries
Equity Share Approach Control Approach (Financial or 
Operational)
Account for emissions in proportion to your % ownership of each operation. Account for 100% of emissions from operations you control — regardless of 
ownership %.
A 40%-owned joint venture contributes 40% of its emissions to your inventory. Financial control: you direct the entity's financial policy. Operational control: 
you direct its operating policy.
Common in investment and holding-company contexts.
The most common approach for corporate operational reporting — including 
BRSR in India.

Scope 1 vs. 2 vs. 3 — Side by Side
Scope 1 & 2 Scope 3
Directly measurable from your own meters, fuel receipts, and utility bills. Estimated from supplier, customer, and market-average data — rarely directly 
metered.
Mandatory under nearly every reporting framework, including BRSR. Increasingly required (CSRD, SBTi) but historically voluntary in many

S E C T I O N 3 O F 7
Scope 1 — Direct Emissions
Emissions from sources you own or control — the most direct entry in the ledger.
16

S E C T I O N 3 · D E F I N I T I O N
Scope 1 — Direct Emissions
GHG emissions from sources owned or controlled by the reporting organization, falling into four categories.
Stationary Combustion
Fuel burned in boilers, furnaces, and 
generators at fixed facilities.
Mobile Combustion
Fuel burned in company-owned or -
leased vehicles — cars, trucks, forklifts.
Fugitive Emissions
Unintentional releases — refrigerant 
(HFC) leaks from AC and cooling systems, 
equipment leaks.
Process Emissions
Released directly by an industrial process 
itself, not combustion — e.g. cement 
calcination, chemical manufacturing.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 17

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E C O R E F O R M U L A
The Universal Emissions Calculation Formula
This same structure — with different activity data and factors — calculates Scope 1, 2, and most of Scope 3.
Emissions (tCO₂e) = Activity Data × Emission Factor ×
GWP
Activity Data
The quantity of a fuel, material, or service consumed —
litres of diesel, kWh of electricity, tonnes of steel, km 
travelled.
Emission Factor
A published, standardized figure converting one unit of 
activity into GHG mass — e.g. kgCO₂e per litre of diesel, 
sourced from IPCC, DEFRA, EPA, or CEA.
GWP
Applied only when the emission factor is not already 
expressed in CO₂e — converts a non-CO₂ gas mass into 
its CO₂-equivalent warming effect.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 18

S E C T I O N 3 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Scope 1: Emissions From Fuel Combustion
G I V E N
Diesel consumed by backup generators: 5,000 litres/year
Petrol consumed by company vehicles: 2,000 litres/year
Emission factor, diesel (typical published factor): 2.68 kgCO₂e/litre
Emission factor, petrol (typical published factor): 2.31 kgCO₂e/litre
F O R M U L A
Scope 1 = Σ (Fuel Volume × Emission Factor) ÷ 1000
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Diesel: 5,000 L × 2.68 kgCO₂e/L = 13,400 kgCO₂e
2 Petrol: 2,000 L × 2.31 kgCO₂e/L = 4,620 kgCO₂e
3 Sum the two sources: 13,400 + 4,620 = 18,020 kgCO₂e
4 Convert kg to tonnes: 18,020 ÷ 1,000 = 18.02 tCO₂e
18.02 tCO₂e Total Scope 1 emissions for the year, from stationary generator combustion plus mobile vehicle combustion combined.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 19

◆ INTERACTIVE P R A C T I C E P R O B L E M
Scope 1: Your Turn
"A campus canteen uses an LPG cylinder-fed cooking system, consuming 600 kg of LPG per year. What are its annual Scope 1 emissions?"
GIVEN: LPG consumption = 600 kg/year; Emission factor for LPG (typical published factor) = 2.98 kgCO₂e/kg
S U G G E S T E D S O L U T I O N
Scope 1 = Activity Data × Emission Factor
600 kg × 2.98 kgCO₂e/kg = 1,788 kgCO₂e
Convert to tonnes: 1,788 ÷ 1,000 = 1.788 tCO₂e
ANSWER ≈ 1.79 tCO₂e per year
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 20

S E C T I O N 4 O F 7
Scope 2 — Energy Indirect Emissions
Emissions from the energy you buy — generated elsewhere, but caused by your consumption.
21

S E C T I O N 4 · D E F I N I T I O N
Scope 2 — Purchased Energy
Indirect emissions from the generation of electricity, steam, heating, or cooling that your organization purchases and consumes.
Why "Indirect" The physical combustion happens at the power plant, not on your premises — but your consumption decision 
causes it.
What Counts Purchased grid electricity is the most common source; purchased steam, heat, and chilled water for cooling also 
fall under Scope 2.
Why It Gets Its Own Scope Purchased energy is significant enough, and different enough from on-site combustion, that the GHG Protocol 
treats it as a distinct category with its own calculation methods.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 22

S E C T I O N 4 · T W O M E T H O D S
Location-Based vs. Market-Based Method
Location-Based Method Market-Based Method
Uses the average emission intensity of the grid(s) where consumption 
physically occurs.
Uses emissions specific to the electricity contracts an organization has actually 
purchased.
In India: the CEA's published grid-average emission factor. Reflects renewable energy certificates (RECs), power purchase agreements 
(PPAs), and green tariffs.
Answers: "How clean is the grid I'm drawing from?" Answers: "How clean is the electricity I chose to buy?"
The same for every company on the same grid. Can fall close to zero if 100% renewable energy is contractually purchased.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 23

S E C T I O N 4 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Scope 2: Using India's Grid Emission Factor
G I V E N
Annual grid electricity consumption: 500,000 kWh (500 MWh)
India weighted average grid emission factor (CEA CO₂ Baseline Database, FY 
2023–24): 0.727 tCO₂/MWh
Method used: Location-based
F O R M U L A
Scope 2 (location-based) = Electricity Consumed (MWh) × Grid 
Emission Factor (tCO₂/MWh)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Convert consumption to MWh: 500,000 kWh = 500 MWh
2 Apply the CEA grid emission factor: 500 MWh × 0.727 tCO₂/MWh = 363.5 tCO₂e
3
Note: if this energy were instead 100% covered by a renewable PPA, market-based Scope 2 could approach 0 tCO₂e — which is exactly why the GHG Protocol requires 
reporting both methods side by side.
363.5 tCO₂e Location-based Scope 2 emissions for the year, using the Central Electricity Authority's published grid-average emission factor.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 24

◆ INTERACTIVE P R A C T I C E P R O B L E M
Scope 2: Your Turn
"A data center consumes 1,200 MWh of grid electricity annually. Calculate its location-based Scope 2 emissions."
GIVEN: Electricity consumption = 1,200 MWh/year; CEA FY 2023–24 grid emission factor = 0.727 tCO₂/MWh
S U G G E S T E D S O L U T I O N
Scope 2 = Electricity Consumed (MWh) × Grid Emission Factor
1,200 MWh × 0.727 tCO₂/MWh = 872.4 tCO₂e
ANSWER 872.4 tCO₂e per year

S E C T I O N 5 O F 7
Scope 3 — Value Chain Emissions
Everything else in the value chain — usually the hardest to measure, and usually the largest.
26

S E C T I O N 5 · D E F I N I T I O N
Scope 3 — Value Chain Emissions
All indirect emissions that occur in an organization's value chain, excluding Scope 2 — both upstream (suppliers) and downstream (customers).
Not Owned, Not Controlled These emissions physically happen at other companies' facilities, in other people's vehicles, or inside products 
after they've been sold.
Why It's Hardest to Measure Reliable data means asking suppliers and customers for their own emissions — data an organization rarely has 
direct access to.
Why It's Still Required For most industries, Scope 3 is 70–90% of the total footprint. Skipping it means missing most of the real number.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 27

S E C T I O N 5 · T H E 1 5 C A T E G O R I E S ( 1 O F 2 )
Upstream Scope 3 — Categories 1 to 8
Everything that happens before a product or service reaches your organization.
1. Purchased Goods & Services
Emissions from producing everything your 
organization buys or acquires.
2. Capital Goods
Emissions from producing purchased long￾term assets — machinery, buildings, 
equipment.
3. Fuel- & Energy-Related Activities
Upstream emissions of fuel and energy not 
already counted in Scope 1 or 2.
4. Upstream Transportation & 
Distribution
Third-party transport of purchased products 
to your organization.
5. Waste Generated in Operations
Emissions from third-party disposal and 
treatment of your operational waste.
6. Business Travel
Employee travel for business in vehicles not 
owned by the organization — flights, trains, 
taxis.
7. Employee Commuting
Emissions from employees' travel between 
home and work.
8. Upstream Leased Assets
Emissions from operating assets you lease, 
not already in Scope 1 or 2.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 28

S E C T I O N 5 · T H E 1 5 C A T E G O R I E S ( 2 O F 2 )
Downstream Scope 3 — Categories 9 to 15
Everything that happens after your product or service leaves your organization.
9. Downstream Transportation
Transport and distribution of sold products, 
after they leave your control.
10. Processing of Sold Products
Emissions from further processing of your 
products by downstream companies.
11. Use of Sold Products
Emissions from customers actually using the 
products you sold — often the largest 
downstream category.
12. End-of-Life Treatment
Emissions from disposal and treatment of 
sold products at the end of their life.
13. Downstream Leased Assets
Emissions from assets you own but lease out 
to others to operate.
14. Franchises
Emissions from the operation of franchises 
not already counted elsewhere.
15. Investments
Emissions financed through equity, debt, and 
project investments — largest for banks and 
asset managers.

S E C T I O N 5 · C H O O S I N G A M E T H O D
Four Ways to Calculate Scope 3
Data availability, not preference, usually decides which method you use — and different categories often need different methods.
Supplier-Specific Method Uses actual emissions data reported by your own suppliers. Most accurate — but requires supplier cooperation 
few companies fully have yet.
Hybrid Method Combines supplier-specific data where available with secondary (industry-average) data to fill the gaps.
Average-Data Method Activity data (mass, distance, count) × an industry-average emission factor — e.g. tonnes of steel × tCO₂e per 
tonne of steel.
Spend-Based Method Money spent × an economic input-output (EEIO) emission factor. Fastest and most available — but the least 
precise; often used as a first screening pass.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 30

S E C T I O N 5 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Scope 3, Category 1: Average-Data Method
G I V E N
Steel purchased for manufacturing: 200 tonnes/year
Industry-average emission factor for crude steel production (e.g. worldsteel 
Association): ≈1.9 tCO₂e per tonne
Method used: Average-data method
F O R M U L A
Category 1 Emissions = Mass of Material Purchased (tonnes) ×
Material Emission Factor (tCO₂e/tonne)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Apply the factor: 200 tonnes × 1.9 tCO₂e/tonne = 380 tCO₂e
2 This covers steel alone — a complete Category 1 figure sums this calculation across every material, component, and service purchased in the year.
380 tCO₂e Category 1 (Purchased Goods & Services) emissions attributable to steel procurement for the year.

Tools, Data & the Indian Context
Where the emission factors come from, who requires this data, and what automates it at scale.

S E C T I O N 7 · D A T A S O U R C E S
Where Emission Factors Actually Come From
Every calculation in this lecture depended on a published, standardized emission factor — these are the primary sources.
IPCC The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change publishes default global emission factors and GWP values used 
as the international baseline.
DEFRA (UK) The UK Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs publishes an annually updated set of GHG conversion 
factors, widely used worldwide as reference data — including the fuel factors used in this lecture.
US EPA The US Environmental Protection Agency's GHG Emission Factors Hub covers fuels, electricity, and materials for 
the US context.
CEA (India) India's Central Electricity Authority publishes the annual CO₂ Baseline Database for the Indian Power Sector —
the authoritative source for India's grid emission factor.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 39

S E C T I O N 7 · W H O R E Q U I R E S T H I S D A T A
Reporting Frameworks Built On These Numbers
The calculation methodology is identical — what changes is who you report it to, and how it gets verified.
CDP (Carbon Disclosure Project) A global voluntary disclosure platform used by investors and customers to assess corporate climate risk and 
performance.
SBTi (Science Based Targets initiative) Requires verified Scope 1, 2, and (increasingly) Scope 3 data before certifying that a company's emissions￾reduction target is scientifically credible.
BRSR (India) SEBI's Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting mandate for India's top 1,000 listed companies by 
market cap — Scope 1 and 2 disclosure required, Scope 3 increasingly expected.
CCTS (India) India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, administered by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, prices emissions directly 
using CEA grid data as its baseline reference.
CAR B ON FOOT P R I N T CALCULAT I ON · SCOP E 1, 2 & 3 40

S E C T I O N 7 · Y O U R A N G L E
What Automates This At Scale
The hand calculations you just did are exactly what carbon accounting software automates across thousands of line items.
Carbon Accounting Platforms Tools like Watershed and Persefoni ingest utility bills, spend data, and supplier records to run this same formula 
automatically, continuously.
Emission Factor APIs Platforms like Climatiq expose emission factor databases as an API, letting developers query "diesel, India, 
2024" and get back a verified factor programmatically.
The Engineering Problem Underneath Every platform like this is, at its core, a data pipeline problem: ingest messy activity data, match it to the right 
emission factor, apply the right GWP, and produce an auditable number.

L E C T U R E R E C A P
The Complete Calculation, Recapped
1
Carbon Footprint
Total GHG emissions from an entity, expressed in tCO₂e using GWP to combine 
different gases.
2
The GHG Protocol
The global standard (WRI/WBCSD) behind every Scope 1/2/3 number reported 
worldwide.
3
Organizational Boundaries
Set first, using either the equity-share or control approach, before any calculation 
begins.
4
Scope 1
Direct emissions from owned or controlled sources — stationary, mobile, fugitive, and 
process.
5
Scope 2
Indirect emissions from purchased energy — calculated via location-based or market￾based methods.
6
Scope 3
15 categories of value-chain emissions, upstream and downstream — usually 70–90% 
of the total.
7
The Universal Formula
Emissions = Activity Data × Emission Factor × GWP — the same structure across all 
three scopes.
8
The Case Study Lesson
A company reporting only Scope 1 and 2 may be capturing roughly one-sixth of its real 
footprint.
9
India's Framework
CEA grid factors, BRSR mandatory disclosure, and the CCTS carbon market all build on 
this exact methodology.
10 Your Opportunity
Every one of these calculations is a data pipeline problem waiting for better software.

Why Carbon Needs a Market
The economic logic that turns an invisible gas into a priced, tradable commodity.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E C O R E P R O B L E M
The Externality Problem
A factory that burns coal doesn't pay for the warming it causes — a third party (the whole planet) bears that cost instead. Economists call this a negative 
externality.
The Market Failure Without intervention, the price of fossil energy reflects only extraction and production cost — never the climate 
damage it causes downstream.
The Economic Fix Put an explicit price on emissions, so the cost of climate damage is "internalized" into the decisions of the 
emitter — exactly what a market failure requires.
Two Ways To Do It Governments have converged on two dominant tools to set that price: taxing emissions directly, or capping total 
emissions and letting a market set the price.
CAR B ON T R ADI N G, P R I CI N G & R I SK MAN AGE ME N T 06

S E C T I O N 1 · T W O P O L I C Y T O O L S
Carbon Tax vs. Cap-and-Trade
Carbon Tax Cap-and-Trade (ETS)
Government sets the price directly; the market determines the resulting 
quantity of emissions.
Government sets the total quantity (the cap) directly; the market determines 
the resulting price.
Simple to administer, highly predictable cost for businesses. Guarantees a specific emissions outcome — the cap is a hard ceiling.
Emissions reduction is uncertain — it depends how businesses respond to the 
price.
Price is uncertain and can be volatile, since it depends on market supply and 
demand.
Examples: Sweden, Canada's federal backstop, Singapore. Examples: EU ETS, California Cap-and-Trade, China National ETS, India's CCTS.

Carbon Pricing Mechanisms

S E C T I O N 2 · P R I C E D I S C O V E R Y
What Actually Sets a Carbon Price?
Unlike a carbon tax, market-based carbon prices emerge the same way any commodity price does.
Auctions Regulators periodically auction newly issued allowances — bidders compete on price, setting a fresh market 
signal.
Secondary Trading Once issued, allowances and credits trade continuously between companies, banks, and traders on exchanges 
like ICE and EEX.
Supply & Demand Fundamentals Economic activity, fuel prices, weather (affecting renewable output), and policy tightening all shift the price, 
exactly like any other commodity.

S E C T I O N 3 O F 7
Compliance Markets (Cap-and-Trade)
The world's largest, most regulated carbon markets — where participation is mandatory, not optional.

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E M E C H A N I C S
How Cap-and-Trade Actually Works
Four steps turn a policy goal into a functioning market.
1. Set the Cap
The regulator sets a hard ceiling on total 
emissions across all covered entities, 
shrinking it year over year.
2. Allocate Allowances
The cap is divided into tradable 
allowances (1 allowance = 1 tonne CO₂e), 
given out free and/or sold at auction.
3. Trade Freely
Companies that cut emissions cheaply 
can sell spare allowances; companies 
facing high abatement costs buy what 
they need.
4. Surrender & Comply
At year-end, each entity must surrender 
one allowance per tonne actually 
emitted — shortfalls trigger penalties.
CAR B ON T R ADI N G, P R I CI N G & R I SK MAN AGE ME N T 15

S E C T I O N 3 · D I S T R I B U T I N G A L L O W A N C E S
Free Allocation vs. Auctioning
Free Allocation Auctioning
Allowances given to companies at no cost, based on historical output or 
benchmarks.
Allowances sold to the highest bidder — companies pay the full market price 
upfront.
Protects industries exposed to international competition from "carbon 
leakage."
Generates government revenue that can fund climate programs (as EU ETS 
auction revenue does).
Risk: can hand out windfall profits if allowances are given generously. Creates a stronger, cleaner price signal from day one — no ambiguity about 
opportunity cost.

S E C T I O N 4 O F 7
Voluntary Markets & Offsets
Where anyone — company or individual — can buy a claim to emissions reduced elsewhere.

S E C T I O N 4 · A C R I T I C A L D I S T I N C T I O N
Carbon Allowances vs. Carbon Credits
Allowances (Compliance) Credits (Offsets)
A permission slip: "the right to emit one tonne," issued under a legal cap. A claim: "one tonne was actually reduced or removed elsewhere," from a 
specific project.
Total supply is fixed by regulation — scarcity is enforced by law. Supply grows whenever a new project is registered and verified — no legal cap.
Value comes from legal scarcity within a mandatory scheme. Value depends entirely on whether the underlying project's claim is actually 
true.
Traded within EU ETS, CCTS, California Cap-and-Trade, etc. Traded on the voluntary carbon market (VCM) — Verra, Gold Standard, and 
others.
CAR B ON T R ADI N G, P R I CI N G & R I SK MAN AGE ME N T 21

S E C T I O N 4 · Q U A L I T Y C O N T R O L
What Makes a Carbon Credit Credible?
A tonne claimed on paper is worthless unless it clears four tests.
Additionality
The reduction would not have happened 
anyway, without the carbon credit 
revenue as an incentive.
Permanence
The carbon stays out of the atmosphere 
for the long term — not released again 
by fire, logging, or reversal.
Verification
An independent third party confirms the 
claimed reduction actually occurred, 
using agreed methodology.
No Double-Counting
The same tonne of reduction is claimed 
by only one buyer, in only one registry, 
exactly once.
CAR B ON T R ADI N G, P R I CI N G & R I SK MAN AGE ME N T 22

S E C T I O N 4 · T H E M A R K E T
Who Runs the Voluntary Carbon Market?
Independent, non-governmental standards bodies certify most voluntary credits — there is no single global regulator.
Verra (VCS) The largest voluntary standard, having issued more than 1 billion carbon credits since 2009 across renewable 
energy, forestry, and other project types.
Gold Standard Founded with WWF backing, known for stricter co-benefit requirements — notably declining to certify credits 
based on avoided deforestation alone.
ACR & CAR The American Carbon Registry and Climate Action Reserve — North America-focused standards with their own 
methodologies and registries.
CAR B ON T R ADI N G, P R I CI N G & R I SK MAN AGE ME N T 23

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When "Verified" Credits Turned Out to Be Phantom
The Guardian / Die Zeit / SourceMaterial Investigation (Jan 2023)
A nine-month investigation found that over 90% of Verra's rainforest (REDD+) offset credits — the most commonly used offset type — were likely "phantom 
credits" that did not represent genuine emissions reductions.
Who Was Exposed
Buyers of the affected credits for climate claims included Disney, Shell, Gucci, Salesforce, 
BHP, and easyJet.
The Specific Failure
The Kariba REDD+ project alone was later found by Verra itself to have issued roughly 15.2 
million "excess" (over-issued) credits.
Verra's Response
Verra disputed the investigation's methodology, but announced it would phase out and 
replace its REDD+ methodology going forward.
The Market Impact
The controversy triggered a broader crisis of confidence in forest-based offsets, and 
accelerated demand for more rigorous, tech-verified credit types.

S E C T I O N 5 · T W O M E C H A N I S M S
How CCTS Actually Works
CCTS is deliberately built as two linked but distinct tracks.
The Compliance Mechanism Energy-intensive sectors are given emissions-intensity targets (tCO₂e per unit of output) — not an absolute cap 
on total emissions.
Why Intensity, Not an Absolute Cap India's economy is still growing fast. An intensity target lets output — and total emissions — rise while still 
forcing each unit of output to get cleaner every year.
The Offset Mechanism Non-covered entities can register eligible projects (renewable energy, green hydrogen, landfill methane capture, 
and more) to earn tradable Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs).
Over-Achievers vs. Under-Performers Companies that beat their intensity target earn and can sell CCCs; companies that miss it must buy CCCs to 
cover the gap, or face a financial penalty.
CAR B ON T R ADI N G, P R I CI N G & R I SK MAN AGE ME N T 28

S E C T I O N 5 · W H O R U N S I T
Sectors & Institutions
Nine sectors, three institutions, one national registry.
Nine Covered Sectors
Aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, 
fertiliser, iron & steel, pulp & paper, 
petrochemicals, petroleum refining, and 
textiles.
BEE (Administrator)
The Bureau of Energy Efficiency 
administers the scheme and sets 
technical standards and procedures.
Grid Controller of India
Operates the Indian Carbon Market 
registry, where every Carbon Credit 
Certificate is recorded and tracked.
CERC (Trading Oversight)
The Central Electricity Regulatory 
Commission oversees trading of CCCs on 
power exchanges (IEX, HPOWERT, PXIL).

G I V E N
A cement plant's FY target: 0.85 tCO₂e per tonne of cement produced
Actual performance achieved: 0.80 tCO₂e per tonne of cement produced
Annual cement production: 1,000,000 tonnes
F O R M U L A
CCCs Earned = (Target Intensity − Actual Intensity) × Production 
Volume
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Intensity improvement: 0.85 − 0.80 = 0.05 tCO₂e saved per tonne of cement
2 Total CCCs earned: 0.05 × 1,000,000 = 50,000 Carbon Credit Certificates
3 These 50,000 CCCs can now be sold on a power exchange to another entity that missed its own target.

Risk Management in Carbon Markets
Every market this lecture has covered carries real financial and reputational risk — here is how to categorize it.
32

S E C T I O N 6 · T H E F O U R C A T E G O R I E S
What Can Actually Go Wrong
Every carbon market participant — buyer, seller, or regulator — faces some mix of these four risk types.
Price / Market Risk
Allowance and credit prices can swing 
sharply on policy news, energy prices, or 
macroeconomic shocks.
Regulatory / Policy Risk
Rules change — caps tighten, 
methodologies get replaced, entire 
schemes get suspended or redesigned 
mid-cycle.
Delivery / Counterparty Risk
A seller may fail to deliver credits or 
allowances as promised, or a registry 
may cancel credits after purchase.
Reputational Risk
Buying low-quality or fraudulent credits 
and making public climate claims on 
them invites "greenwashing" 
accusations.

S E C T I O N 6 · M A N A G I N G P R I C E R I S K
Hedging Instruments in Carbon Markets
Large emitters rarely just buy allowances on the spot market — they manage exposure the way any commodity trader would.
Futures Contracts Standardized exchange contracts (e.g. on ICE) to buy or sell allowances at a fixed price on a future date —
locking in compliance cost in advance.
Forwards Similar to futures but privately negotiated between two parties — more flexible, but carries more counterparty 
risk since it isn't exchange-cleared.
Options The right (not the obligation) to buy or sell allowances at a set price — insurance against extreme price moves, 
paid for with an upfront premium.
Why This Matters A cement plant with a €1M+ annual compliance cost cannot simply hope the price stays low — these 
instruments turn an unpredictable cost into a manageable, budgetable one.

S E C T I O N 6 · T H E R E P U T A T I O N A L R I S K L E S S O N , R E V I S I T E D
Greenwashing Is Now a Legal and Financial Risk
The Verra case from Section 4 is a textbook example of reputational risk crystallizing into real financial and legal consequences.
1. The Claim
A company buys cheap rainforest credits 
and publicly claims "carbon neutral" 
status based on them.
2. The Exposure
Independent journalism or academic 
research finds the underlying credits 
don't represent real reductions.
3. The Consequence
Regulators, NGOs, and litigators 
increasingly treat unsupported climate 
claims as consumer-protection or 
securities violations.
4. The Lesson
Credit quality due diligence is no longer 
optional risk management — it is now 
core to avoiding legal and reputational 
exposure.

S E C T I O N 7 · G O I N G G L O B A L
Article 6 & Linking Markets Together
The Paris Agreement includes a specific mechanism for countries to cooperate and trade emissions reductions across borders.
Article 6 of the Paris Agreement Establishes rules for countries to transfer emissions reductions between each other, and for a new UN￾supervised crediting mechanism.
Market Linking Separate schemes (like the EU ETS and Switzerland's ETS) can be formally linked, letting allowances flow 
between them and converging their prices.
Why This Matters As more national schemes like CCTS mature, the long-term direction is toward more interconnected, more liquid 
global carbon markets — with all the opportunity and risk that implies.

Carbon Markets Run on Infrastructure You Could Build
Every mechanism in this lecture — trading, verification, registries — is, underneath, a data and software problem.
MRV Technology Satellite monitoring and remote sensing increasingly cross-check offset project claims — directly addressing the 
exact failure mode behind the Verra scandal.
Blockchain Registries Distributed ledgers are being piloted to prevent double-counting and give buyers an auditable, tamper-evident 
credit history.
AI-Assisted Fraud Detection Machine learning models can flag anomalous credit issuance patterns — the kind of over-issuance that took 
investigative journalists nine months to uncover by hand.
The Opportunity Carbon market integrity is currently a trust problem waiting for better engineering — exactly the kind of gap this 
course keeps returning to.

The Externality Problem
